deep.reconstruction:
This page is part of the long table in E283 (written 1762, published 1764) giving the prime divisors of a^2+1 for a = 1 to 1500. It covers a = 696 to 753. The purpose of the paper is to find very large primes. A number a^2+1 is prime exactly when it has no prime factor up to a. The admissible prime factors are only 2 (for odd a) and primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4). Euler finds them by a sieve on the roots of x^2 ≡ -1 (mod p). If p divides r^2+1, then p divides (r+kp)^2+1 and (kp−r)^2+1 for every k, so each p strikes out two arithmetic progressions of a. The listing convention, confirmed by checks on this page, is as follows. An entry lists every prime factor of a^2+1 below a, together with any second factor above a when the factorization closes exactly. Whatever is left over is a single prime greater than a, since a^2+1 can have at most one prime factor exceeding a. A blank entry means a^2+1 itself is prime. Blanks on this page are a = 696, 700, 704, 714, 716, 740, 750. These agree with the modern list of n for which n^2+1 is prime (OEIS A005574): 484417, 490001, 495617, 509797, 512657, 547601, 562501. Some entries are complete factorizations:
- 697^2+1 = 2·5·13·37·101
- 701^2+1 = 2·17·97·149
- 703^2+1 = 2·5·73·677
- 717^2+1 = 2·5·101·509
- 731^2+1 = 2·397·673
- 743^2+1 = 2·5^2·61·181
- 746^2+1 = 13^2·37·89
- 748^2+1 = 5·317·353
Others leave a prime cofactor, for example:
- 698^2+1 = 5·97441
- 706^2+1 = 41·12157
- 715^2+1 = 2·255613
- 726^2+1 = 601·877
- 744^2+1 = 17·32561
- 749^2+1 = 2·13·21577
The residue pattern is visible in the table: 2 divides a^2+1 exactly for odd a, and 5 exactly for a ≡ 2, 3 (mod 5). 5^2 appears for a ≡ 7, 18 (mod 25), i.e. at 707, 718, 732 and 743. The large primes Euler wanted are the cofactors (a^2+1)/(listed divisors), which run to roughly 5.7·10^5 on this page.
errors: None found in spot checks. Every product and complete factorization tested agrees with a^2+1, and the cofactors tested (97441, 12157, 255613, 3457, 6793, 2281, 1913, 4889, 14561, 39877, 32561, 21577, 6653, 877, 937, 1789, 1373) are prime. All blank entries agree with the known list of n with n^2+1 prime.

ideas.what: A table of the prime factors of a^2+1 for a up to 1500, built by sieving with the roots of x^2 ≡ -1 mod p for primes p ≡ 1 mod 4, used to exhibit large primes as a^2+1 or as cofactors (a^2+1)/d.
ideas.modern_name: Sieve factorization of the polynomial values n^2+1; primes of the form n^2+1 (Landau's fourth problem); largest prime factor of n^2+1
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, E283 (1762/1764); tables later extended by Cunningham and others; the asymptotic questions are due to Chebyshev, Landau and Hooley
ideas.where_published: E283, Novi Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Petropolitanae 9 (1764); Opera Omnia I.3

ideas.what: Implicit principle: a^2+1 has at most one prime factor greater than a, so once all divisors up to a are removed, the leftover cofactor is prime.
ideas.modern_name: Trial division bound / at most one prime factor exceeding sqrt(N)
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore; used explicitly by Euler in this paper

deep.surprise_reason: This is a purely tabular page of a well-known, published and cited Euler table. The entries checked are correct and the method is the documented one. Nothing here is new to the literature.
transcription_corrections: The header in the image reads 'Diuisores ipsius aa+1' with long-s ('Diuiſores ipſius'); the transcription has 'Diuifores ipfius'.
717: the image shows '2. 5. 101 509' with the period missing before 509; the intended entry is 2·5·101·509.
The catchword at the bottom of the page is '754'; the signature mark is absent or illegible here, unlike 'S 2' on the previous page.
